# Attendance Scanner – devlog

> A compact, standalone barcode terminal for tracking school club attendance. Students scan the barcode on their existing school ID card, and the terminal sends the scan over Wi-Fi to a backend server that records attendance (to be built later). The whole device sits on a single custom PCB. An ESP32-S3 microcontroller handles Wi-Fi and control, a dedicated barcode scanner module reads the cards, and a small display, buzzer, and status LEDs give instant feedback on whether the scan worked. It runs on a rechargeable LiPo battery, charges over USB-C, and keeps working while plugged in, so you can carry it to any club meeting without needing an outlet.

## Design

### 2026-10-06 – Started working on the schematic of the power system. Working from the USB-C receptacle to the static protector, to the charger chip, to the battery socket. It allows the power to come in from the usb

**1.5h**

Started working on the schematic of the power system. Working from the USB-C receptacle to the static protector, to the charger chip, to the battery socket. It allows the power to come in from the usb-c, with proper static protection as this can be missused. The charger chip is to charge the battery. The battery socket is where the battery will plug into. Also including the necessary resistors and capacitors.

![Hour1Schematic](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/37a4a4ca32cd981a41ec15ac722aca5a618ff97c3494bba1e93b5bf2ca92b75e.png)

![Hour1Schematic-3](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/78b9a5998e6bf5ca5f93a9e0cf92eefe5469264a049d272daf72118b68cca2e9.png)

### 2026-10-07 – Finally finished the schematic. I first worked on making sure the power block was done. I ran the ERC on that specifically, and it had like 2 errors that needed to be fixed, but those were pretty easy

**5h**

Finally finished the schematic. I first worked on making sure the power block was done. I ran the ERC on that specifically, and it had like 2 errors that needed to be fixed, but those were pretty easy to fix.

![ERCWithErrors](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/976a8c8f9b180fdbe5eb051c7eb4e93f9621b6f8903b18bbd73f42f3f6e16911.png)

It was basically, since I am just using a battery socket and a usb - c receptacle, KiCad didn't know where I was getting power from. So I just added power flags to the VSYS, GND, and VBUS tags so KiCad recognizes I am supplying power through those.

![PowerFlag](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/e151f03ef457634b3ed3f432a5654a848fedfd0130acb3e6026781c949a3eae4.png)

Next, I worked on getting the ESP32 hooked up. For detecting battery voltage, since the battery goes up to 4.2V and the pin used to detect battery voltage on the ESP32 can handle up to 3.3v, I used 2 identical resistors to split the voltage in half, so in the software I can just double whatever input I get from that pin. I also used a tiny capacitor to smooth the inputs to the pin.

![BatterySensorResistorSetup](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/0d831e3737ae023eab7f81a731f7e293aab0d213fbabc736e62aab28772ebc75.png)

Then I added the 6-pin connector for the barcode scanner; the 4-pin connector for the OLED screen; the buzzer and transistor, which is needed to amplify the voltage; and the red and green status LEDs.

Finished Schematic:
![SchematicDone](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/55dc1d167fe906d8aa7b20a248be3cc1325abf940fd71e778c7226b66c768505.png)

No errors left in the Electrical Rules Checker (ERC) tool:
![ERCNoErrors](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/bf7be44c65298eac0d95ea8b35082335549afbfd770409d9ff15759fa0f23d0c.png)

### 2026-10-07 – I restarted the entire schematic. I was talking to a close friend about the topic and telling him how much added complexity the power system adds and how I was thinking of making it run just on USB-C.

**4h**

I restarted the entire schematic. I was talking to a close friend about the topic and telling him how much added complexity the power system adds and how I was thinking of making it run just on USB-C. Initially, I wanted to avoid that, but the complexity was just too high for me to continue with the schematic I had previously made. It was heavily influenced by tutorials, and it was too complex for my skill level (beginner). He told me that some boards already have built-in power management systems, so they will handle that for you. I realised that if I plan to actually make this project usable, I will need to use these boards. I researched and found the Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32S3

![SeeedStudioXiaoBoard](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/49a884df2a1e71a64534fe61f27e0bf84c3270fa6f818f62f0f2b38f5bd9347b.png)

With this new board, it was easier to restart the whole schematic than to go and delete my individual work. Since I removed some complexity there, I also switched to an RGB LED because that is something I have never used before and wanted to try using.

![V2InitialMicroControllerSchematic](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/8f04c3829785d3684de924544acad61fe3fa92b12f90d950625a7e83efb9a7ab.png)

Then I worked on adding in the buzzer. I used fewer net labels this time, so it is easier for me to visualize what connects to what and where; this time, without the use of any tutorials (AI was used to check over my work to make sure I wasn't breaking it, but only after using the ERC).

![V2CleanerBuzzerSchematic](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/eb55d47de1929452f3b9cbab6dcfb9ce79aabeaa34c99c23d3f5ed116e6921b8.png)

Then adding the screen was pretty simple; I had to add my own pull-down resistors, but I knew how to do that. The barcode scanner was also very similar to the previous version, so I could easily make that without any help. And the same for the power switch. It still took me a while overall because I am still pretty inexperienced and had to restart more than once because I was doing something wrong. Now the schematic is finished!

![v2DoneSchematicNoBatterySense](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/18f858be3578aa89ac3cabb82670db9e50e1ecac12a7ddaeb3f3df07fa941636.png)

### 2026-10-10 – I started selecting the specific components I wanted to use so I could select the correct footprints. I basically only used AliExpress and then made sure the footprints on the schematic matched the ac

**5h**

I started selecting the specific components I wanted to use so I could select the correct footprints. I basically only used AliExpress and then made sure the footprints on the schematic matched the actual components. Then I moved on to actually getting the schematic into the PCB. I started arranging it, but then I realised that I wasn't accounting for stuff like the screen and how you can't have bigger components sitting underneath that. I also had to decide how I wanted the actual case to look and how the users would interact with the scanner and the LEDs and stuff. Here is what I initially had:

![PCBArrangement1](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/b0f08e088369752ab27dfb8f6db99cec5d2d104e7720f3be83110221f83367d1.png)

Then I took some time to figure out how I wanted my case to look, how I wanted the user to interact with the scanner, and stuff. I decided the PCB was going to be angled upward, and the USB-C port would be out from the top. So after 2-3 tries, this is what I ended up with (The big square is the screen, the resistors are small enough to fit underneath):

![PCBFinalArrangement](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/c86fcc1c7272083a108288719ac9db493a227470e37e05c55af49a0147e5e96a.png)

Then I did the routing; that took a while, and it is pretty messy. I might take some time to clean up the routing. I also added a GND zone fill to both the top and bottom layers. Here is the schematic:

![PCBZoneFilled](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/f936f885b897b8b11df8cd4ffb0f57e2e353b1da61fc6e6ea31960166fd9e1c5.png)
